t.7.76.1: Having heard those words of Lakṣmaṇa, the destroyer of foes said to Lakṣmaṇa, "Tell me in full the slaying of Vṛtra."
t.7.76.2: Thus addressed by Rāghava, Lakṣmaṇa, who increased the joy of Sumitrā, once again narrated a divine tale.
t.7.76.3: Having heard the words of the thousand-eyed one and of all the heaven-dwellers, Viṣṇu spoke this to all the gods, who had Indra at their head.
t.7.76.4: Formerly I was bound in friendship to the most great-souled Vṛtra; therefore, even for the sake of pleasing you, I will not slay the great asura.
t.7.76.5: Your supreme happiness must certainly be brought about; therefore I shall tell you the means by which you will slay Vṛtra.
t.7.76.6: O best of the gods, I shall make myself threefold; by that means the thousand-eyed one will slay Vṛtra, there is no doubt.
t.7.76.7: Let one portion go to Vāsava, the second to the thunderbolt, and the third to the earth; then Śakra will slay Vṛtra.
t.7.76.8: When the lord of the gods spoke thus, the gods then said these words: "It is just so, there is no doubt, as you say, O slayer of Daityas."
t.7.76.9: May good fortune be yours! We shall go, eager for the slaying of the asura Vṛtra. O most noble one, support Vāsava with your own splendour.
t.7.76.10: Then all those great-souled ones, with Sahasrākṣa at their head, approached that forest where the great asura Vṛtra was.
t.7.76.11: They beheld that foremost of asuras, become radiant with splendour and blazing forth, as though drinking up the three worlds and as though burning up the sky.
t.7.76.12: And at the very sight of that foremost of asuras, the gods were seized with terror: "How shall we slay him? How may we escape defeat?"
t.7.76.13: While they were deliberating there, the thousand-eyed Puraṃdara grasped the vajra with both arms and hurled it at Vṛtra's head.
t.7.76.15: Pondering the slaying of that Vṛtra, which seemed impossible, the illustrious lord of the gods went swiftly to the end of the world.
t.7.76.14: Scorched as if by the dreadful fire of the world's end, as if by a blazing, mighty flame, the world was seized with terror at what befell Vṛtra's head.
t.7.76.16: As Indra hurried away, Brahmahatyā, the sin of slaying a brahmin, swiftly followed him; she fell upon his limbs, and sorrow entered Indra.
t.7.76.17: Their enemy slain but their Indra vanished, the gods, with Agni at their head, worshipped Viṣṇu, the foremost of the three worlds, again and again.
t.7.76.18: You are the supreme refuge, O god, the first-born and lord of the world; for the protection of all beings you have taken on the nature of Viṣṇu.
t.7.76.19: This Vṛtra has been slain by you, and the sin of brahmin-slaying now torments Vāsava. O tiger among the gods, show the way to his release.
t.7.76.20: Having heard those words of the gods, Viṣṇu said: "Let Śakra worship me alone; I shall purify the wielder of the thunderbolt."
t.7.76.21: Having worshipped me with the holy horse-sacrifice, Pākaśāsana, free from fear on every side, will once again attain the lordship of the gods.
t.7.76.22: Having thus conveyed to the gods that nectar-like speech, Viṣṇu, the lord of the gods, went to heaven while being praised.
